criteria.descriptor: Full marks: SLI is correctly a good/valid event ratio measured near the user; 'valid' correctly excludes client 4xx/429; TTFT (not total latency) is correctly chosen and justified for streaming; error budget is correctly the complement of the SLO; burn rate is correctly defined as budget-consumption rate and the multi-window scheme is technically sound. Deduct for wrong SLI math, treating total latency as fine, mislabelling SLI/SLO/SLA, or a broken/hand-wavy burn-rate definition.

Full marks: addresses all four required parts (SLI good/valid definition, SLO + error budget, error-budget policy, burn-rate alerting) AND explicitly explains both the too-much and too-little failure modes of the p99 monitor. Deduct for each missing part (e.g. no error-budget policy, no explicit good/valid criteria, only one of the two p99 failure modes).

Full marks: choices are justified by mechanism (why TTFT rather than total time; why exclude client errors; why a budget rather than zero-errors; why multi-window balances detection vs precision vs reset) rather than asserted. Deduct where recommendations are stated without a causal 'because'.

Full marks: organised by the four requested parts, uses correct vocabulary (SLI/SLO, error budget, burn rate, TTFT, valid vs good events) precisely, and is concise. Deduct for disorganised, ambiguous, or jargon-dropping-without-meaning prose.

expected_answer_points: Defines the SLI as a ratio of good events to valid (total) events measured close to the user (LB/gateway) from raw events, not a server-side average or pre-aggregated percentile

Specifies 'valid' events to exclude client-caused errors (e.g. 4xx / 429 quota rejections) so the service is not penalised for callers' faults, and defines 'good' concretely (2xx, and a completed stream for /chat)

Argues the streaming latency SLI should be time-to-first-token (or inter-token latency), and explains that total response latency is wrong because it scales with output length and conflates verbosity with degradation
Sets a concrete SLO target over a rolling window (e.g. 99.9% / 28 days) and derives the error budget as the complement, framing the budget as a spendable resource; avoids 100%/unrealistic targets
Defines an error-budget policy: a concrete consequence when the budget is exhausted (e.g. freeze risky launches/rollouts, prioritise reliability) that ties the SLO to action
Proposes multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting, explaining burn rate as the rate of budget consumption, with a fast high-burn page (short+long window pair) and a slow-burn ticket alert
Explains why the static p99 monitor both over-pages (short harmless spikes, no duration/impact link, alert fatigue) and under-pages (sustained sub-threshold degradation drains budget undetected)
common_pitfalls: Choosing total response latency (or total-time p99) as the streaming SLI, not recognising it scales with generated token count and so conflates a legitimately long answer with a degradation; the correct signal is time-to-first-token and/or inter-token latency

Keeping a static threshold alert ('page when latency/error-rate > X') without tying it to an error budget, so it stays disconnected from user impact and duration and reproduces the alert-fatigue problem
Counting client-caused errors (4xx, 429 quota rejections) as bad events in the SLI, burning the budget and paging on-call for faults the service did not cause

Conflating SLA (external, contractual, penalty-bearing) with SLO (internal target) and SLI (the measured metric), or setting a 100%/99.999% SLO that leaves no error budget and guarantees constant paging

Proposing a single-window burn-rate alert, which is either too slow to catch a fast outage or too noisy on brief spikes, instead of a multi-window multi-burn-rate scheme that balances detection time, reset time, and precision
Explaining only one side of the p99 monitor's failure (usually the over-paging) and missing that a sustained sub-threshold degradation silently drains the budget without ever tripping the monitor
reference_answer:
SLI definition. An SLI should be a ratio of good events to valid events computed from raw request logs at the point closest to the user (load balancer / API gateway), never a pre-aggregated server-side average. I would define two families:

- Availability SLI: fraction of valid requests that return a successful response out of all valid requests. 'Valid' excludes client-caused 4xx such as 400/401 and 429 rate-limit rejections, because burning our budget on the caller's own quota or malformed input punishes us for things outside our control. 'Good' = 2xx, and for /chat specifically a stream that completes (first token AND clean end-of-stream), so half-finished streams count as bad.
- Latency SLI: for the streaming /chat endpoint the meaningful signal is time-to-first-token (TTFT) — fraction of requests whose first token arrives within a threshold (e.g. 2s). Total response time is the wrong SLI here because it grows with output length: a legitimate 2000-token answer takes longer than a 20-token one, so a total-latency SLI conflates model verbosity with degradation and will look 'slow' whenever answers are long. Optionally add an inter-token latency / tokens-per-sec SLI for steady-state throughput. /embeddings, being synchronous, can use ordinary request latency.

SLO and error budget. Set a target over a rolling window, e.g. 99.9% of valid requests good over 28 days. The complement (0.1%) is the error budget — the quantity of bad events we may spend. The point is the budget, not 'zero errors': it turns reliability into a measurable, spendable resource. Avoid 100% or 99.999% targets that leave no room to ship and guarantee constant paging.

Error-budget policy. Agree in advance what happens when the budget is exhausted: freeze risky launches / model-weight rollouts and redirect effort to reliability until it recovers. This ties the SLO to a decision rather than leaving it a vanity dashboard.

Burn-rate alerting. Alert on how fast the budget is being consumed (burn rate = observed bad-rate divided by the bad-rate that would exactly exhaust the budget over the SLO window). Use multi-window, multi-burn-rate: a fast/high-burn page (e.g. ~14.4x burn = 2% of a 30-day budget in 1h) gated by a short 5-minute second window so it fires only while the incident is live and resets quickly; plus a slow-burn ticket-only alert (~1-3x over 6h/24h) to catch gradual erosion.

Why the p99 monitor fails. 'p99 > 3s for 5 min' isn't tied to user impact or duration, so it pages on a harmless 2-minute spike (the nighttime noise) yet a sustained latency sitting just under 3s silently drained the budget for hours last week (the missed degradation). It also encourages invalid percentile-averaging across instances and leaves the aggregation window ambiguous. Burn-rate alerting scales urgency to actual budget consumption and gives predictable detection and reset behavior.
